Question 1 of 20, Level 1

1MCQ1 mark
A cylindrical tank is being filled with sand at the rate of 314 m3/h314\ \text{m}^3/\text{h}314 m3/h. If the radius of the tank is 101010 m, then the height of sand in the tank increases at the rate of: (Take π=3.14\pi = 3.14π=3.14)

Tap the option you think is right.

Work it out on paper first. Then reveal the solution one step at a time.

Formula / idea Volume of a cylinder V=πr2hV = \pi r^2 hV=πr2h; here rrr is fixed, only hhh changes.

  1. 1

    Write the volume with r=10r = 10r=10 m.

    V=π(10)2h=100πhV = \pi (10)^2 h = 100\pi hV=π(10)2h=100πh
  2. 2

    Differentiate w.r.t. ttt.

    dVdt=100π dhdt\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 100\pi\,\dfrac{dh}{dt}dtdV​=100πdtdh​dVdt=100π dhdt\displaystyle \dfrac{dV}{dt} = 100\pi\,\dfrac{dh}{dt}dtdV​=100πdtdh​
  3. 3

    Put dVdt=314\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 314dtdV​=314 and π=3.14\pi = 3.14π=3.14.

    314=100(3.14)dhdt  ⇒  dhdt=314314=1 m/h314 = 100(3.14)\dfrac{dh}{dt} \;\Rightarrow\; \dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{314}{314} = 1\ \text{m/h}314=100(3.14)dtdh​⇒dtdh​=314314​=1 m/h314=100(3.14)dhdt  ⇒  dhdt=314314=1 m/h\displaystyle 314 = 100(3.14)\dfrac{dh}{dt} \;\Rightarrow\; \dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{314}{314} = 1\ \text{m/h}314=100(3.14)dtdh​⇒dtdh​=314314​=1 m/h
    1
  4. 4

    Match with the options.

    Option (B)\text{Option (B)}Option (B)
Answer(B) 1\displaystyle 11 m/h

Watch out Treating rrr as a variable too. The tank's radius is fixed, so only hhh is differentiated.

Question 2 of 20, Level 1

2MCQ1 mark
The function f(x)=x3−3x2+3x−100f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 3x - 100f(x)=x3−3x2+3x−100 is:

Tap the option you think is right.

Work it out on paper first. Then reveal the solution one step at a time.

Formula / idea If f′(x)≥0f'(x) \ge 0f′(x)≥0 and f′(x)=0f'(x) = 0f′(x)=0 only at isolated points, fff is strictly increasing.

  1. 1

    Differentiate.

    f′(x)=3x2−6x+3f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x + 3f′(x)=3x2−6x+3
  2. 2

    Factorise.

    f′(x)=3(x2−2x+1)=3(x−1)2f'(x) = 3(x^2 - 2x + 1) = 3(x - 1)^2f′(x)=3(x2−2x+1)=3(x−1)2
  3. 3

    A square is never negative.

    f′(x)≥0 for all x∈Rf'(x) \ge 0 \ \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}f′(x)≥0 for all x∈Rf′(x)≥0 for all x∈R\displaystyle f'(x) \ge 0 \ \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}f′(x)≥0 for all x∈R
  4. 4

    f′(x)=0f'(x) = 0f′(x)=0 only at x=1x = 1x=1, so fff is increasing on R\mathbb{R}R.

    Option (A)\text{Option (A)}Option (A)
    1
Answer(A) increasing on R\displaystyle \mathbb{R}R

Watch out Choosing (C) because f′(1)=0f'(1) = 0f′(1)=0. One isolated zero of f′f'f′ does not stop fff increasing.

3MCQ1 mark
The interval in which f(x)=x2−4x+6f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 6f(x)=x2−4x+6 is strictly decreasing is:

Tap the option you think is right.

Work it out on paper first. Then reveal the solution one step at a time.

Formula / idea fff is strictly decreasing where f′(x)<0f'(x) < 0f′(x)<0.

  1. 1

    Differentiate.

    f′(x)=2x−4=2(x−2)f'(x) = 2x - 4 = 2(x - 2)f′(x)=2x−4=2(x−2)
  2. 2

    Find where f′(x)<0f'(x) < 0f′(x)<0.

    2(x−2)<0  ⇒  x<22(x - 2) < 0 \;\Rightarrow\; x < 22(x−2)<0⇒x<2
  3. 3

    So fff is strictly decreasing on (−∞,2)(-\infty, 2)(−∞,2).

    Option (A)\text{Option (A)}Option (A)
    1
Answer(A) (−∞,2)\displaystyle (-\infty, 2)(−∞,2)

Watch out Picking (2,∞)(2, \infty)(2,∞): there f′(x)>0f'(x) > 0f′(x)>0, so fff is increasing, not decreasing.

6Assertion-Reason1 mark
Assertion (A): f(x)=sin⁡xf(x) = \sin xf(x)=sinx is strictly increasing in (0,π2)\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)(0,2π​). Reason (R): If f′(x)>0f'(x) > 0f′(x)>0 for every xxx in an open interval, then fff is strictly increasing in that interval.

Tap the option you think is right.

Work it out on paper first. Then reveal the solution one step at a time.

Formula / idea Theorem: f′(x)>0f'(x) > 0f′(x)>0 on an open interval ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ fff is strictly increasing there.

  1. 1

    Check A: f′(x)=cos⁡x>0f'(x) = \cos x > 0f′(x)=cosx>0 for 0<x<π20 < x < \tfrac{\pi}{2}0<x<2π​. So A is true.

    f′(x)=cos⁡x>0 in (0,π2)f'(x) = \cos x > 0 \ \text{in} \ \left(0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)f′(x)=cosx>0 in (0,2π​)f′(x)=cos⁡x>0 in (0,π2)\displaystyle f'(x) = \cos x > 0 \ \text{in} \ \left(0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)f′(x)=cosx>0 in (0,2π​)
  2. 2

    Check R: it is the standard theorem in NCERT. So R is true.

  3. 3

    A follows directly from R using f′(x)=cos⁡x>0f'(x) = \cos x > 0f′(x)=cosx>0. So R explains A.

  4. 4

    Hence the correct option is (A).

    Option (A)\text{Option (A)}Option (A)
    1
Answer(A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

Question 7 of 20, Level 1

7Short answer2 marks
The edge of a cube is increasing at the rate of 333 cm/s. How fast is the volume increasing when the edge is 101010 cm long?

Work it out on paper first. Then reveal the solution one step at a time.

Formula / idea Rate of change: dVdt=dVdx⋅dxdt\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{dV}{dx} \cdot \dfrac{dx}{dt}dtdV​=dxdV​⋅dtdx​ (chain rule).

  1. 1

    Let edge =x= x=x cm and volume =V= V=V. Given rate:

    V=x3,dxdt=3 cm/sV = x^3, \qquad \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3\ \text{cm/s}V=x3,dtdx​=3 cm/sV=x3,dxdt=3 cm/s\displaystyle V = x^3, \qquad \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3\ \text{cm/s}V=x3,dtdx​=3 cm/s
  2. 2

    Differentiate w.r.t. ttt.

    dVdt=3x2dxdt\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 3x^2 \dfrac{dx}{dt}dtdV​=3x2dtdx​
    1
  3. 3

    Put x=10x = 10x=10 and dxdt=3\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3dtdx​=3.

    dVdt=3(10)2(3)=900\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 3(10)^2(3) = 900dtdV​=3(10)2(3)=900
    ½
  4. 4

    State the result with units.

    Volume increases at 900 cm3/s\text{Volume increases at } 900\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}Volume increases at 900 cm3/sVolume increases at 900 cm3/s\displaystyle \text{Volume increases at } 900\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}Volume increases at 900 cm3/s
    ½
AnswerThe volume is increasing at 900 cm3/s\displaystyle 900\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}900 cm3/s.

Watch out Writing the unit as cm/s. The rate of volume is in cm3/s\text{cm}^3/\text{s}cm3/s.

Find the intervals in which f(x)=2x3−3x2−36x+7f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 36x + 7f(x)=2x3−3x2−36x+7 is (a) strictly increasing (b) strictly decreasing.

Work it out on paper first. Then reveal the solution one step at a time.

Formula / idea f′(x)>0⇒f'(x) > 0 \Rightarrowf′(x)>0⇒ strictly increasing; f′(x)<0⇒f'(x) < 0 \Rightarrowf′(x)<0⇒ strictly decreasing.

  1. 1

    Differentiate.

    f′(x)=6x2−6x−36f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 36f′(x)=6x2−6x−36
  2. 2

    Factorise.

    f′(x)=6(x2−x−6)=6(x−3)(x+2)f'(x) = 6(x^2 - x - 6) = 6(x - 3)(x + 2)f′(x)=6(x2−x−6)=6(x−3)(x+2)f′(x)=6(x2−x−6)=6(x−3)(x+2)\displaystyle f'(x) = 6(x^2 - x - 6) = 6(x - 3)(x + 2)f′(x)=6(x2−x−6)=6(x−3)(x+2)
    1
  3. 3

    Put f′(x)=0f'(x) = 0f′(x)=0.

    x=−2orx=3x = -2 \quad \text{or} \quad x = 3x=−2orx=3
    ½
  4. 4

    These points split the real line. Check the sign of f′(x)f'(x)f′(x) in each part.

    IntervalSign of f′(x)Nature of f(−∞,−2)(−)(−)>0strictly increasing(−2,3)(−)(+)<0strictly decreasing(3,∞)(+)(+)>0strictly increasing\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Interval} & \text{Sign of } f'(x) & \text{Nature of } f \\ \hline (-\infty, -2) & (-)(-) > 0 & \text{strictly increasing} \\ (-2, 3) & (-)(+) < 0 & \text{strictly decreasing} \\ (3, \infty) & (+)(+) > 0 & \text{strictly increasing} \end{array}Interval(−∞,−2)(−2,3)(3,∞)​Sign of f′(x)(−)(−)>0(−)(+)<0(+)(+)>0​Nature of fstrictly increasingstrictly decreasingstrictly increasing​​

    Signs shown are of (x−3)(x - 3)(x−3) and (x+2)(x + 2)(x+2).

    ½
  5. 5

    (a) Strictly increasing on

    (−∞,−2)∪(3,∞)(-\infty, -2) \cup (3, \infty)(−∞,−2)∪(3,∞)
    ½
  6. 6

    (b) Strictly decreasing on

    (−2,3)(-2, 3)(−2,3)
    ½
Answer(a) Strictly increasing on (−∞,−2)∪(3,∞)\displaystyle (-\infty, -2) \cup (3, \infty)(−∞,−2)∪(3,∞); (b) strictly decreasing on (−2,3)\displaystyle (-2, 3)(−2,3).

Watch out Factorising x2−x−6x^2 - x - 6x2−x−6 as (x+3)(x−2)(x + 3)(x - 2)(x+3)(x−2). Check: (x−3)(x+2)=x2−x−6(x - 3)(x + 2) = x^2 - x - 6(x−3)(x+2)=x2−x−6.

    At x=1x = 1x=1: f′′f''f′′ is negative, so local maximum.

Work it out on paper first. Then reveal the solution one step at a time.

Formula / idea Quotient rule: (uv)′=vu′−uv′v2\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)' = \dfrac{v u' - u v'}{v^2}(vu​)′=v2vu′−uv′​; sign of f′(x)f'(x)f′(x) decides increasing or decreasing.

  1. 1

    Note the domain: log⁡x\log xlogx needs x>0x > 0x>0.

    Domain=(0,∞)\text{Domain} = (0, \infty)Domain=(0,∞)
  2. 2

    Differentiate by the quotient rule.

    f′(x)=x⋅1x−log⁡x⋅1x2=1−log⁡xx2f'(x) = \dfrac{x \cdot \frac{1}{x} - \log x \cdot 1}{x^2} = \dfrac{1 - \log x}{x^2}f′(x)=x2x⋅x1​−logx⋅1​=x21−logx​f′(x)=x⋅1x−log⁡x⋅1x2=1−log⁡xx2\displaystyle f'(x) = \dfrac{x \cdot \frac{1}{x} - \log x \cdot 1}{x^2} = \dfrac{1 - \log x}{x^2}f′(x)=x2x⋅x1​−logx⋅1​=x21−logx​
    1
  3. 3

    Put f′(x)=0f'(x) = 0f′(x)=0.

    1−log⁡x=0  ⇒  log⁡x=1  ⇒  x=e1 - \log x = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \log x = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; x = e1−logx=0⇒logx=1⇒x=e1−log⁡x=0  ⇒  log⁡x=1  ⇒  x=e\displaystyle 1 - \log x = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \log x = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; x = e1−logx=0⇒logx=1⇒x=e
    ½
  4. 4

    x=ex = ex=e splits the domain into (0,e)(0, e)(0,e) and (e,∞)(e, \infty)(e,∞). Note x2>0x^2 > 0x2>0 always.

    Sign of f′(x)=sign of (1−log⁡x)\text{Sign of } f'(x) = \text{sign of } (1 - \log x)Sign of f′(x)=sign of (1−logx)Sign of f′(x)=sign of (1−log⁡x)\displaystyle \text{Sign of } f'(x) = \text{sign of } (1 - \log x)Sign of f′(x)=sign of (1−logx)

Work it out on paper first. Then reveal the solution one step at a time.

Formula / idea Similar triangles link the shadow sss to the distance xxx; then differentiate w.r.t. ttt.

  3. 3

    dsdt=12×5=52 km/h\dfrac{ds}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 = \dfrac{5}{2}\ \text{km/h}dtds​=21​×5=25​ km/hdsdt=12×5=52 km/h\displaystyle \dfrac{ds}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 = \dfrac{5}{2}\ \text{km/h}dtds​=21​×5=25​ km/h

20Case study4 marks
Case Study: A technical company is designing a rectangular solar panel installation on a roof using 300300300 metres of boundary material. The design includes a partition running parallel to one of the sides, dividing the area into two sections. Let the length of the side perpendicular to the partition be xxx metres and the side parallel to the partition be yyy metres.
  1. (i)Write the equation for the total boundary material used (boundary and partition) in terms of xxx and yyy.1 mark
  2. (ii)Write the area of the solar panel as a function of xxx.1 mark
  3. (iii)(a)Find the critical point of the area function and use the second derivative test to find the maximum area.2 marks
  4. OR
  5. (iii)(b)Using the first derivative test, find the maximum area the company can enclose with the 300300300 m of boundary material.2 marks

Work it out on paper first. Then reveal the solution one step at a time.

Formula / idea Use the material constraint to write area in one variable, then apply the derivative test.

(i)1 mark

  1. 1

    The boundary has two sides of length xxx and two of length yyy.

    Boundary=2x+2y\text{Boundary} = 2x + 2yBoundary=2x+2y
    ½
  2. 2

    The partition is parallel to the yyy sides, so its length is yyy. Total:

    2x+2y+y=300  ⇒  2x+3y=3002x + 2y + y = 300 \;\Rightarrow\; 2x + 3y = 3002x+2y+y=300⇒2x+3y=3002x+2y+y=300  ⇒  2x+3y=300\displaystyle 2x + 2y + y = 300 \;\Rightarrow\; 2x + 3y = 3002x+2y+y=300⇒2x+3y=300
    ½
Answer (i)2x+3y=300\displaystyle 2x + 3y = 3002x+3y=300

(ii)1 mark
